The critic's finding: DRE-6930's thread memo is keyed on (count, max id, max edited_at), but the store rewrites event rows in place (author, author_kind, previous, external_id) without moving any of the three, so the "nothing stale is shown" claim is false. What the re-plan changed: The second critic sent this plan back with five findings on 2026-10-11. Every one is answered in this revision. No card was added and none was removed: the six cards are the same six, two rewritten and two extended.

**What changed, card by card.**

The thread-memo card (DRE-6930) is rewritten. The critic found that the memo could show a stale comment or lane move: the database rewrites a thread's rows in place when it fills in who wrote a comment or what lane a card came from, and the memo's old check could not see those rewrites. The card now lists every way the backend writes to a thread (ten of them) and gives the memo a check that moves on each one, with a test replaying each case and a guard test that fails if a new way of writing is ever added without being covered. The card also says plainly the one case the check cannot see, and why nothing writes that case today, instead of claiming nothing stale is ever shown.

The board-rows card (DRE-6928) is rewritten. It strips the card body out of the rows the board reads, keeping it only where a card declares a short name. The critic found the way the card spelled that filter would have crashed every board read in production (the production database driver reads a percent sign as a placeholder) while the local tests stayed green. The filter is now passed as a value rather than written into the query, a test exercises the production dialect, and the list of columns the board keeps is read off the table itself rather than copied by hand, so a column added later cannot drop out.

The operator card (DRE-6927) gains one step and one criterion: the record it writes on DRE-6585 now carries an "Instance decision" paragraph stating the service's configured instance counts, that the one-server-or-two question is the CEO's and is asked outside this epic, and that no stack card is filed here.

The proof card (DRE-6931) gains one row: the record quotes that paragraph and lists the epic's cards with the statement that none touches the backend stack, so the epic's fourth criterion is answered in the proof's own table.

**The five findings, in the critic's order.**

1. The memo's check missed in-place rewrites of thread rows, so "nothing stale is shown" was false. FIXED: the check now reads every column a thread serves, every writer is enumerated and replayed in a test, a guard test catches new writers, and the card states the one boundary the check has rather than an absolute claim.

2. The specific rewrite paths (the lane-history fill, the comment-identity fill, and the re-ingest that fills actor columns) needed a replay test each. FIXED: the replay list names each of those paths as its own case, including the fill of each column separately and the out-of-order edit a simpler check would miss.

3. The short-name filter would crash board reads on the production database, and the column list was hand-written. FIXED: the filter is a bound value, a production-dialect test asserts no stray percent sign reaches the driver, and the column list is read off the table with a test that adds a column and sees it appear.

4. The instance decision was recorded only in the plan comment, with no card or proof row carrying it. FIXED: the operator card writes it on DRE-6585 as an "Instance decision" paragraph, and the proof record quotes that paragraph and lists the cards in its own criterion table.

5. The three store cards share files and are serialized, which the critic confirmed is correct, and the operator card touches nothing. LEFT, with nothing to change: this finding records that the ordering is right. The plan document now states the chain and names it as a serialization, and it records that no open card in the other in-flight epics touches these files.

Nothing here needs a decision from you. Once the second critic passes this revision the plan reaches you for a green light. Plan for DRE-6589, written against the diagnostic reading on DRE-6585 (2026-10-11), as the operator asked.

**Where we stand.** The thing that was shutting the console down is already fixed. The reading found the server holding 4,140 to 4,969 MB with four pages open while the program's own data was about 161 MB; one free setting (live since 03:47 PT on 2026-10-11) brought the same four pages down to 1,352 to 1,674 MB. What is left is the slower part the reading named: every console refresh pulls whole tables into memory — every open card's full comment history (154 MB a refresh), every child of every epic with its full card body (66 MB), every card in a lane with its body (48 MB) — and two views fetch every card ever finished just to count them. These grow with the tables and are the next ceiling. This plan bounds them.

**What gets built, in order.** Six cards, four of them code, about two days of agent work end to end.

1. A reading. The backend writes one log line per board read saying how big it was, once a minute per kind. This ships first so the fix is measured in production, not guessed: the reading that found the sites came from a tracer that froze the server for 28 seconds and could only report once.
2. Lighter rows. The board stops fetching each card's full written body on every refresh. The one place the board reads that text (the short name an epic shows) keeps it; the card's flyout is unchanged.
3. Counting without fetching. Three places that fetch every finished card to count them ask the database for the count instead.
4. Remembering threads. A card's comment history is fetched again only when it has changed, under a fixed memory budget, and checked against the database every time it is served so nothing stale is shown. This is the largest card and the one that removes the 154 MB read.
5. An operator reading, in parallel: the stall that followed each kill on 2026-10-10 — a fresh server answering 3 to 46 requests a minute for ten minutes — is read off the server's own minute-by-minute metrics and explained on the record. The reading did not see a stall, so this is the card the epic asked for in that case.
6. The proof: four console pages held open for an hour on the released build, with every board read under its bar, the server under 3,072 MB, and no kill in the window. One hour rather than two: the operator set that bar on 2026-10-11, and the proof run itself has a two-hour limit.

**What could go wrong.** Card 4 keeps data between refreshes, so its risk is showing a stale comment; it checks every thread against the database before serving it and is tested against every way a thread changes. Card 2 could drop text some screen needed; the places that read it were listed and tested before this plan was written. Card 1 costs a little processor time; it is sampled to one line a minute. Everything is one pull request and reverts cleanly. Nothing here changes the database schema or the servers.

**Two things recorded, not built.** The question of one server or two stays yours and is on your list separately; the operator asked that it not be folded in here, so no server card is filed. Your signed answer on this card (2026-10-10 10:58 PT) agreed to wait for the reading and was not a two-instance decision. Going back from the 6 GB stopgap server to 4 GB is a decision after a week of ordinary daytime use, outside this epic.

To start the build: move ONLY this epic to In Progress — the children promote automatically, in order. Do not move the children by hand.
